Bait check

Fast pass/fail for a CTA, caption line, or pinned-comment trigger. Run
any closing line through this before shipping. If it fails on any of
the first six, rewrite. See `references/anti-patterns.md` for the
underlying logic.

Fail conditions

- [ ] Asks for the **act** of engagement, not the **content**.
      ("Comment YES" vs "tell me what you'd do.")
- [ ] Contains a phrase named or shape-matched as bait: "like for part
      2", "comment YES", "tag a friend", "double-tap if", "share with
      [number] friends", "follow for more", "drop a heart if".
- [ ] Uses a number to demand engagement: "tag 3 friends", "share with
      5 people".
- [ ] Promises a payoff that requires the act of commenting/liking to
      get ("comment YES for the link").
- [ ] Stacks multiple asks: like + save + share + follow + comment.
- [ ] Bait-and-switch: caption promises a free thing, the link or DM
      delivers a sales page.
- [ ] Sits in the closing seconds with no value moment before it.

If any of the above is true, the CTA is bait-shaped. Rewrite.

TikTok

```
VISIBLE LINE (≤ ~80 chars, the headline):
[hook tension or payoff. keyword in the first 100–150 chars.]

BODY (optional, total 50–150 chars):
[context or second hook. avoid echoing the on-screen text.]

PRIMARY KEYWORD: [used once, early]
SECONDARY TERMS (1–2):
  - [term 1]
  - [term 2]

HASHTAGS (3–5, niche, ByteDance-style):
  #[niche-tag] #[niche-tag] #[niche-tag]
  (optional: 1 topical/trending tag if it genuinely fits)

PRIMARY ACTION (one): [save / send / reply-with-video / comment stance]
CTA PLACEMENT: [5s before known drop-off, or around the 70% mark]
```

Quick reuse checklist

- [ ] Visible line lands before the platform's cutoff.
- [ ] Primary keyword appears once, early.
- [ ] Hashtag count matches the platform (3–5; #Shorts on YouTube).
- [ ] One primary action, not three.
- [ ] Caption doesn't echo the on-screen hook verbatim.
- [ ] Run through `bait-check.md` before shipping.

Matrix

| Content type | Primary action | Why it fits |
|---|---|---|
| Tutorial / how-to | Save | Viewer will need it later |
| List / round-up | Save | Reference content |
| Recommendation / review | Send | "You need to see this" travels |
| Story / personal | Send | Specific person comes to mind |
| Demo / before-after | Save or send | Recipe vs "look at this" |
| Opinion / hot take | Comment with stance | Real debate fuels the section |
| Cliffhanger to long-form | Watch full video | The Short is the trailer |
| Pure entertainment | None (let it loop) | Asking taxes a working video |

Save (tutorial, list, how-to)

- "Save this before your next [specific moment]."
- "Save this for the next time you [predictable future situation]."
- "If you're saving these, the third one is the one nobody does."
- Implicit, said mid-video at a peak: "if you're writing this down..."

Placement

- Layered is best: implicit prompt at the 70% mark, explicit prompt
  near the end.
- Data-driven version: open Insights or Analytics, find the actual
  drop-off, place the primary CTA about 5 seconds before it.
- Never lead with a CTA. CTAs land when they ride a value moment.

A. Objection-killer

Take the predictable critical comment off the board.

```
Yes, [the obvious objection]. I tested [the specific case] and
[the honest result].
```

Example skeletons:

- "Yes, this works on oily skin too. I tested it for 14 days."
- "Before you say 'sponsored': I bought all three myself."
- "I've had three people ask if it works on [X]. Yes, same routine,
  same result."

Putting the CTA before the payoff

Asking for a save in second three, before the viewer has any reason to
want to save it. CTAs land when they ride a value moment. Placed
before the value, they trigger skip behaviour.

The pattern that works: deliver the payoff (or a real taste of it),
**then** make the ask. See `ctas-that-work.md` on placement.

Bait-and-switch caption-to-DM

Caption promises a "free guide", the auto-DM sends a $297 course sales
page. Triggers spam reports, kills trust, and repeated bait-and-switch
flows are part of what gets accounts demoted under spammy-behaviour
enforcement.

The rule: whatever the caption promises, the DM delivers, first,
before any pitch.

Treating the caption as an afterthought

A one-emoji caption on Instagram leaves the search-discovery channel
completely off, in a feed where the caption is the SEO surface. The
fix isn't a long caption. It's any caption that contains the topic
words a real person would type into search.

Caption craft

The caption is the layer the algorithm reads as text, and the layer the viewer
reads before deciding to tap. It does two jobs at once: SEO and persuasion.
Optimise for both, in that order, per platform.

Instagram (Reels and posts)

- Hard cap: 2,200 characters.
- Visible portion before "...more": about 125 characters, roughly 18 to 20
  words.
- Sweet spot for total length: 138 to 150 characters. Long captions exist
  (story-led posts, controversial takes) but the default is short.
- The first 125 characters are functionally a headline. If they don't earn
  the tap, the rest of the caption may as well not exist.
- Captions are the primary SEO signal. Mosseri has stated this directly:
  hashtags do not boost reach, captions do.

TikTok

- Hard cap: 4,000 characters.
- Visible portion before truncation: roughly 80 to 100 characters.
- High-engagement captions cluster in the 50 to 150 character range.
- The caption is one of six categorisation inputs the algorithm reads
  (alongside hashtags, music, effects, location/language, and transcript).
- Keyword in the first 100 to 150 characters gets the video ranked for
  in-app search.

YouTube Shorts

- Title hard cap: 100 characters. Only about 40 show on the feed tile.
- Description hard cap: 5,000 characters. First 100 to 125 characters appear
  before "Show more".
- Title and the first 125 chars of description are direct ranking signals,
  the same way they are on long-form.
- Auto-captions are used for search and for auto-translate to 100+
  languages, so a clear voiceover extends international reach for free.

The first-line rule

The visible portion before the cutoff is a headline. Write it as one. The
rules:

- Lead with the **payoff or the tension**, not with setup or throat-clearing.
- Open a **curiosity gap**: pose a question, a contradiction, or a
  confession the viewer can't resolve without watching or tapping.
- Concrete beats vague. A number, a named thing, a stakes word.
- A 7-word hook with a real information gap tends to outperform a 20-word
  hook that over-explains.
- Stacked-hook formulas (visual hook + verbal hook + on-screen text within
  the first 1.5 seconds) tend to lift early retention.

Map the CTA to the content

| Content type | Primary action | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Tutorial / how-to / list | Save | The viewer wants to come back to it |
| Story / recommendation / review | Send | "You need to see this" travels in DMs |
| Opinion / hot take | Comment with stance | Real debate fuels the comment section |
| Cliffhanger from a longer piece | Watch full video | The Short is the trailer |
| Demo / before-after | Save or send | Depends on whether it's a recipe or a "look" |

Pick one. Earn the action.

Save-driving CTAs

Saves are one of the few cases where an explicit ask correlates with
the metric. Best on content the viewer might actually need later.

Patterns:

- "Save this for your next trip."
- "Save this before your next sourdough attempt."
- "Save this. You'll want it when [predictable future moment]."
- Implicit: "if you're saving these..." said at a peak moment in the
  middle of the video.

The trick is naming the **specific future moment** the save pays off.
Generic "save for later" lifts less than "save for the next time you
panic at a restaurant menu".

CTA placement

End-card CTAs assume completion, but most viewers exit before the final
frame. Practical pattern:

- **Layered**: a light implicit prompt at the 70% mark ("if you're
  saving these..."), plus an explicit closing prompt.
- **Data-driven version**: open Insights or Analytics, find the actual
  drop-off point, and place the primary CTA about 5 seconds before it.
- For loops and rewatches, the closing CTA can be a line that loops
  back to the hook, so the rewatch is the CTA.

Open question vs instruction

Open questions ("what would you have done?") drive comment volume but
rarely beat instruction CTAs ("save this before your next trip") on
the metric that lifts reach (saves and sends). Use open questions when
the topic is genuinely debate-worthy. Default to instruction CTAs tied
to the content's utility.

Check the CTA against the bait shapes

Before shipping, run the CTA through `assets/bait-check.md`. The most
common rewrites:

- "Comment YES for the link" → put the link in the pinned comment.
- "Tag a friend" → "send this to the one friend who [specific
  situation]."
- "Follow for more X tips" → cut it. Replace with a save or send.
- "Like if you agree" → cut it.
- "Share this with everyone" → "send this to your [specific person]."

YouTube Shorts

- Hashtags act as topic and category signals.
- Put **3 to 5 hashtags in the description**, not in the title. The
  first three description hashtags auto-appear above the title as
  clickable links anyway, so burning title characters on them is
  wasted space.
- **`#Shorts` is the one required hashtag.** It signals to YouTube
  that the video is eligible for the Shorts feed.
- Hard cap: **15 hashtags total per video**. Go above 15 and YouTube
  ignores all of them. Absolute ceiling is 60 across all metadata
  before active penalty.

**Working pattern:** `#Shorts` + 2 to 4 niche tags in the description.
Done.

Pinned comments

The pinned comment is a second surface most creators leave empty. It
extends watch time, answers the obvious question before it's asked,
carries the link or list that didn't fit, and seeds the direction of
the comment section. On Instagram especially, it's one of the cheapest edits you
can make to a published post for the lift it delivers.

Instagram (the strong case)

- You can pin **your own** comments, up to **three per post or Reel**.
- Ordering quirk: when three are pinned, the most recently pinned shows
  first and the oldest shows third. Order matters.
- The pinned comment is highly visible: it sits above the rest and
  often shows in the comment preview on the feed.
- Pin from your own account, immediately after publishing, before the
  comment section fills up.

2. Objection-killer

Pre-empt the predictable critical comment. Take it off the board so it
doesn't dominate the section.

Examples:

- "Yes, this works on oily skin too. I tested both."
- "Before you say 'sponsored': I bought all three."
- "Not affiliate, not paid. The brand doesn't know I exist."

Comment-to-DM automation, with eyes open

Comment-to-DM via Meta's official API is supported on Instagram (tools
like ManyChat, Spur, Inrō). Practical caps: about 200 automated DMs
per hour, and you can only DM users who engaged in the last 24 hours.

The trade-off: the visible "comment YES for the link" caption that
triggers the automation is exactly the phrase Meta classifies as
engagement bait. You bank automation conversions while paying a
distribution tax on the host post.

Two mitigations:

- Phrase the trigger as a **topical word**, not a yes/no: "comment
  ROUTINE for the steps" reads less bait-shaped than "comment YES".
- **Deliver what you promise** in the DM, immediately, before any
  pitch. Bait-and-switch DM funnels get reported and demoted.

Timing

- Pin the comment **before** the post goes anywhere. The first 30 to
  60 minutes of a post's life are when the pin works hardest.
- If a comment from another viewer (the perfect objection-killer, a
  great question) shows up later, you can swap it in.
- Edit the pinned comment as the conversation develops. The pin is not
  set-and-forget.

4  | [ARCHETYPE]     | [SPOKEN LINE, <2s]      | [3-7 WORDS]     | [WHAT THE EYE SEES]   | [ONE LINE: WHY THIS]
5  | [ARCHETYPE]     | [SPOKEN LINE, <2s]      | [3-7 WORDS]     | [WHAT THE EYE SEES]   | [ONE LINE: WHY THIS]

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

BACKUP TO A/B:      # [N]
FILM PLAN:          shoot top pick + one backup; read first-3s retention to choose
```

Archetype shorthand to use in the grid:

- `CONTRARIAN`     break the consensus
- `INVESTIGATOR`   "I found a hidden thing"
- `EXPERIMENTER`   "I did X to find out Y"
- `TEACHER`        "X person hit Y using Z method"
- `MAGICIAN`       visual-led, "look at this"
- `FORTUNETELLER`  near-future stakes claim
- `WITHHOLD`       show the result, hold the product
- `STAKES`         "stop doing X if you want Y"
- `CALLOUT`        "if you [situation], this is for you"
- `COST-CONFESS`   "I spent [cost] so you don't have to"
- `IN-MEDIA-RES`   start mid-action, explain after
- `NUMBER-LEAD`    big concrete number first

Notes:

- One archetype per row, no two rows on the same archetype unless the
  execution is meaningfully different.
- If two rows look like rewordings of each other, cut one and replace
  with a new archetype.
- Pair this with `assets/hook-checklist.md` once the batch is drafted.

Hook checklist

Run every candidate hook through this. A strong hook clears most of the
boxes. If it fails the first three, rewrite before going any further.

For the archetype menu, see `references/hook-archetypes.md`. For
common failure modes, see `references/hook-anti-patterns.md`.

Anti-pattern sweep

- [ ] **No welcome / logo / channel intro.**
- [ ] **No "hey guys" or "today we're going to talk about."**
- [ ] **No vague tease without a defined shape.**
- [ ] **No subscribe ask before any value lands.**
- [ ] **No story opener on TikTok.** ("Let me tell you about the time…")
- [ ] **No imperative command** ("stop scrolling") unless the payoff
      earns the urgency.

Three-layer hook worksheet

Fill this in before shooting. The point is to pressure-test that the
visual, verbal, audio, and on-screen text layers all point at the same
idea. A misaligned three-layer hook reads as confused; an aligned one
reads as inevitable.

For the longer explanation, see `references/three-layer-hook.md`.

```
VIDEO IDEA:
ARCHETYPE:           (see references/hook-archetypes.md)
PLATFORM:            (TikTok / Reels / Shorts)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
LAYER          | CONTENT                              | LANDS BY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
VISUAL         | [WHAT THE FIRST FRAME SHOWS]         | second 0
               | [WHY IT WORKS PAUSED]                |
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
VERBAL         | [SPOKEN LINE, 5-10 WORDS]            | second 2
               | [POWER VERB? CONCRETE NOUN?]         |
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ON-SCREEN TEXT | [3-7 WORDS, BIG AND BOLD]            | second 0-1
               | [COMPRESSES VERBAL, DOESN'T REPEAT]  |
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
AUDIO          | [BEAT DROP / CUT TO SILENCE / SOUND] | second 1-2
               | [WHAT IT TIMES TO]                   |
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

Pressure tests

Before shooting, run all four:

- [ ] **Muted test.** Cover the audio. Does the first frame plus the
      on-screen text deliver the hook? If no, the visual or text is
      doing too little.
- [ ] **Eyes-away test.** Cover the visual. Does the spoken line pull
      a glancing viewer back? If no, the verbal hook is too soft.
- [ ] **Glance test.** Look at the frame for half a second, then look
      away. Did the on-screen text register? If not, it's too long or
      too small.
- [ ] **Alignment test.** Do all three layers point at the same idea,
      or are they three different hooks competing? If competing, pick
      the strongest and align the other two to it.

After shooting

Watch the first 3 seconds back without context. Ask:

- Did the hook resolve by second 3?
- Would a stranger swipe in the first half-second?
- If two viewers watched (one with sound, one muted), would both get
  the hook?

If any answer is "no," re-shoot the opener before publishing.

Welcome / logo / channel intro

"Hey guys, welcome back to my channel."

Why it fails: every frame of throat-clearing is a frame of swipe. The
algorithm doesn't wait for the hook to warm up. The Shorts feed and
the Reels algorithm both punish delay in the hook delivery, and
viewers swipe before the actual content begins.

The fix: cut the intro entirely. Open on the payoff frame. If the
creator has a recognizable face, the face is the brand. They don't
need to name themselves at second zero.

Logo animations and channel jingles

Visual equivalent of the welcome intro. A two-second logo before the
content is a two-second flat line on the retention graph.

The fix: branding goes at the end, not the start. The first frame
sells the watch. The end frame sells the channel.

Subscribe-before-value

"Smash that subscribe button before we start." "Follow for more
content like this."

Why it fails: asking for the sub before delivering any payoff creates
psychological resistance. The viewer hasn't earned anything yet, so
the ask reads as presumptuous. Measurable retention drop in the
first three seconds. On Shorts specifically, the subscribe button
sits at the bottom of the player and accidental taps are common,
which means a "subscribe" CTA gets noise rather than signal.

The fix: deliver the value first. The right early CTA on short-form
is "watch the full video on my channel" or "save this for later,"
not "subscribe."

Story openers on TikTok

"Let me tell you about the time I…" "So basically, a few years ago…"

Why it fails: the format pulls in long-form context that the swipe-
decision window can't carry. Storytelling can work on TikTok, but
the hook has to lead with the punchline of the story or the stakes,
not the chronology.

The fix: open on the most arresting moment of the story. Walk back
to setup after. If the story has no moment arresting enough to open
on, it might not be a TikTok.

Hook treated as ornamental

The script gets written first. The hook gets bolted on at the end
as a "catchy opener."

Why it fails: hooks that aren't part of idea-evaluation tend to
fail because they're a coat of paint on a video that didn't earn
attention in the first place. MrBeast's process and Galloway's
both treat hook-writability as part of idea-validation. If you
can't write a sharp hook for the idea, the idea probably isn't
ready.

The fix: write the hook before you write the script. If you can't
write three credible angles, kill the idea or reframe it until you
can.

Single-layer hook

The verbal line is sharp. The first frame is a static face waiting to
talk. No on-screen text.

Why it fails: most viewers watch muted. Without text, the verbal hook
is invisible. Without a working visual frame, the viewer swipes before
the voice lands.

The fix: design all three layers (visual, verbal, text) before
shooting. See `references/three-layer-hook.md` and
`assets/three-layer-worksheet.md`.

How to use this list in critique mode

When the user hands over a draft:

1. Read the hook out loud. Time it. If it runs over 2 seconds, that
   alone is the diagnosis.
2. Check it against this list. Name the specific anti-pattern by
   name. "This is a vague-tease hook" is more useful than "this
   is weak."
3. Rewrite the hook in two or three variants the user can A/B. Don't
   just flag the problem.
4. If the same anti-pattern shows up across multiple drafts from the
   same user, point out the pattern. It's usually one habit, not
   ten separate mistakes.

See `assets/hook-checklist.md` for a pass-fail check to run after
rewriting.

Justin Welsh: the three-line hook

Built for feed posts where only the first two or three lines show
before the "see more" cut. Translates cleanly to short-form on-screen
text and verbal cadence.

Format: three short lines, broken by line breaks, ending on a teaser
that earns the click to keep watching.

Reusable template: *"The [relatable enemy] is [negative thing]. The
[hero] is [strong positive]. And I [accelerant]. [Teaser question]?"*

Welsh's most-copied title stem: **"X [lessons / things / mistakes] I
wish I knew before I [did Y]."** It's portable across niches because
the structure carries the hook, not the topic.

Paddy Galloway: click-to-unpause, packaging plus opener

Two related claims worth applying as one system.

- **The first three seconds decide.** His Shorts teardowns put the
  retention difference between break-out and flop in the first three
  seconds, not later.
- **Click-to-unpause.** The thumbnail or first frame depicts a scene
  mid-action, so the viewer's instinct is to play to see what happens
  next. Compose the opening frame as if it has just been paused.

The split he names: the thumbnail and title sell the click. The first
thirty seconds sell the watch. Everything after that is the show. The
hook is a system that spans both sides of the click.

Choosing the right archetype for an idea

A few shortcuts when matching idea to archetype:

- **Product or result video** with a clear visual payoff: Magician or
  In-media-res (lead with the result frame, explain after).
- **Education or how-to**: Teacher, Hormozi's "How to X without Y," or
  Investigator (you found something the viewer didn't know to look
  for).
- **Strong, defensible opinion**: Contrarian or Fortuneteller. Only
  reach for these if the payoff actually defends the claim.
- **Long, expensive, or visible effort**: Experimenter or Bush's
  big-number lead. The effort is the credibility.
- **Cold audience or paid ad**: Hook-Story-Offer, with the offer
  softened on cold organic.
- **Newsletter or carousel translated to video**: Welsh's three-line
  hook adapted to on-screen text plus voiceover.

When a batch has three or four archetypes represented, the user can
pick the angle that fits the video, not just the wording. That's the
real point of generating across archetypes.

TikTok

The hook window is roughly 1.5 to 3 seconds. The algorithm decides
fast. Most underperforming TikToks fail in the first three seconds,
not later.

What works:

- **Authority + curiosity + payoff promise, resolved by second 3.**
  Credibility in second one ("I've spent six years in [field]"),
  curiosity gap in second two ("the real reason isn't [common
  answer]"), payoff promise in second three ("it's actually [hint]").
  All three resolve before the algorithm finishes the early read.
- **Product or outcome showcase, lead with the finished thing.**
  Outperforms storytelling openers by a meaningful margin. Show the
  result first, explain after.
- **Specific (often odd) numbers.** "$413 burned" reads more measured
  than "$400."
- **Contrarian opens.** The brain struggles to leave a contradiction
  unresolved.

What underperforms:

- Story openers ("let me tell you about the time…").
- "Hey guys, today we're going to talk about…"
- Vague teases ("you won't believe what happened").
- Anything that takes more than 3 seconds to resolve.

On-screen text style:

- Three to seven words. High contrast. Center or upper-third.
- TikTok's UI sits on the bottom and right. Keep text out of those
  zones.
- The native font reads as native. Custom fonts can read as ad.

Sound:

- Trending sound, when it fits, signals freshness. When it doesn't,
  it's noise.
- Original audio is fine for talking-head; the spoken hook is
  indexed for search, so the verbal line is also discovery copy.

Instagram Reels

The hook window is tight. A large share of viewers drop in the first
three seconds. The algorithm reads early dropoff as a signal that the
video isn't worth promoting further.

What works:

- **Visual-led hooks.** Reels rewards strong first-frame composition
  more than TikTok does. A muted, paused-thumb viewer should get the
  hook from the frame alone.
- **A 60% or higher 3-second hold rate.** That's the benchmark a
  strong hook tends to clear. Above 70% tends to unlock broader
  distribution to non-followers.
- **Tight on-screen text in the first frame.** Reels viewers often
  scroll fast; the text earns the pause before the voice lands.
- **Carousel-style "first slide is the hook" thinking.** Reels lives
  in a feed that's heavy on static visuals, so the hook frame should
  read like a strong feed post.

What underperforms:

- Same anti-patterns as TikTok, plus:
- Recycled TikTok exports with the TikTok watermark. Reels' ranking
  appears to demote them.
- Long captions in the first frame. Reels readers don't read past
  the first line.

On-screen text style:

- Bigger and bolder than TikTok. The Reels UI is less crowded but the
  feed competes with high-production carousels.
- Keep the text out of the right-side action rail.

Pacing:

- Slightly slower cuts than TikTok work because Reels viewers
  tolerate a half-beat more setup. Slightly. The hook still has to
  resolve fast.

Long-form YouTube (for comparison)

The cold open serves a different job: validate the click, reduce
time-to-value, and signal that the rest of the video will pay off.
The practical window is 15 to 30 seconds, longer than short-form,
because the viewer has already committed by clicking.

What works:

- A cold open that shows the most arresting moment of the video
  before the title card.
- A first-minute retention curve that escalates rather than ramps.
- The MrBeast-style "minute 0-1 maximum hook intensity, then
  re-engagement spike at minute 3, then payoff" shape.

What underperforms:

- Sponsor reads in the first 7 seconds.
- Logo intros and channel jingles.
- Long autobiographical setups.

The hook on long-form is a system, not a single line. The thumbnail
and title do the pre-click work. The cold open does the post-click
work. Both are part of the same hook system.

Specific numbers, especially odd ones

Round numbers feel made up. Oddly specific numbers feel measured.

- "I tested 47 lipsticks" reads more honest than "I tested 50 lipsticks."
- "$413 on coffee gear" reads more measured than "$400 on coffee gear."
- "11 hooks I write before every video" beats "10 hooks…" by a margin
  that's small per video and meaningful across a batch.

The reason: a precise number implies a count actually happened. A round
one implies an estimate. Curiosity peaks slightly when the brain notices
the precision and asks why.

Numbers also stretch the on-screen text. "$413" in the corner sells the
hook even when the voice is muted.

Authority signals in second one

A short line that establishes credibility before the curiosity gap opens
tends to outperform a curiosity gap alone.

Shape: *"I've spent [time/effort] doing [thing]. Here's what nobody
actually says about it."*

Examples by niche:

- "I've worked in specialty coffee for 8 years. The real upgrade isn't
  the machine."
- "I've shot 200 product videos for skincare brands. The hook everyone
  copies is the wrong one."
- "I've spent six years inside [industry]. The real reason [outcome]
  isn't [common answer]."

Why it works: credibility in second one, curiosity in second two,
implied payoff in second three. All three resolve before the algorithm
finishes its early read.

The risk: false authority reads worse than no authority. If you can't
back the claim, don't make it.

Direct callouts to the exact viewer

Naming the viewer narrows reach but spikes relevance. Reach is what the
algorithm gives you; relevance is what makes the algorithm decide to
give you more.

Shape: *"If you [specific situation], this is for you."*

- "If you've got combination skin and oily T-zone, your toner is the
  problem."
- "If you've posted ten Reels and none broke 1,000 views, this is the
  fix."

When the callout is precise enough, the viewer feels seen in the first
second. Save rate climbs because the viewer mentally bookmarks the video
even before the payoff.

The failure mode: callouts so broad they apply to no one in particular
("if you want to grow on social media…"). The narrower, the better.

In-media-res openers

Start in the middle of the action. Skip the setup. Explain after.

- Demo videos: open on the result. The viewer sees the after, then the
  voice walks back to the before.
- Process videos: open on the most visually arresting moment, then
  rewind.
- Story videos: open on the punchline of the story, then go back to
  setup.

Works because the visual carries the hook, freeing the verbal line to
do the curiosity gap.

Repeat the hook in the on-screen text, compressed

If the verbal hook is "I spent four hundred dollars on coffee gear so
you can skip to the $39 one," the on-screen text isn't the same
sentence. It's "$400 -> $39." Three or four words that sharpen the
spoken line.

Compression rules:

- Drop the verbs.
- Drop the articles.
- Keep the numbers.
- Keep the contrast (the "vs," the arrow, the before/after).

A muted viewer should be able to read the on-screen text and get the
hook in one glance.

Why all three matter

- A large share of short-form views happen on mute. If the verbal hook
  carries the whole promise and there's no caption, most viewers see a
  silent face and swipe.
- The eye registers a visual before the brain finishes parsing a
  spoken sentence. Pre-attentive processing fires inside the first
  half-second. The first frame has to do work before the first
  syllable lands.
- Captions tend to lift completion on short-form by a measurable
  amount versus the same video without them. Treat captions as
  required, not optional polish.

The visual layer

What the eye gets in the first frame.

- **Show the payoff or the conflict.** A finished result, a strong
  emotion, a side-by-side, the after of a before-after. Not a static
  face waiting to begin.
- **Compose for paused-player legibility.** The first frame should
  read the moment a viewer's thumb pauses on the feed. If it needs
  the next two seconds to make sense, it's not a hook frame.
- **Use motion as a pattern interrupt.** Movement, a sudden zoom, a
  jump cut, a hand entering frame. Anything that breaks the rhythm
  of the surrounding feed.
- **Click-to-unpause framing.** Compose the opening frame as if it
  has just been paused mid-action. The viewer's instinct is to play
  to see what happens next.
- **No logo, no countdown, no fade-in.** Every frame of throat-
  clearing is a frame of swipe.

If the only difference between your first frame and the next creator's
is the face, your visual hook isn't doing work yet.

The verbal layer

What the voice says.

- **Five to ten words.** Short enough to land before second 2. The
  spoken line is also indexed for search on most platforms, so it
  doubles as discovery copy.
- **Lead with the payoff or the stake.** "Your $300 coffee setup is
  why it tastes worse" lands. "Hey everyone, today I want to talk
  about coffee" doesn't.
- **One claim, said once.** No setup, no autobiography, no "so
  basically." If the verbal hook needs a sentence of warm-up, the
  warm-up was the real hook. Start there.
- **Use power verbs.** "Burned" not "spent." "Cracked" not "figured
  out." Verbs imply motion and stakes; weak verbs imply a meeting.
- **Match the energy of the visual.** A high-stakes line on a slow
  static shot reads as disjointed. The voice has to live where the
  eye is.

Designing all three together

Practical order for drafting:

1. **Write the verbal line first.** It's the easiest to test by
   reading out loud. Cut until it's under 2 seconds.
2. **Design the visual to land before the voice does.** The first
   frame either shows the payoff, the conflict, or the stake. If
   the voice has to explain what we're looking at, the visual
   isn't pulling weight.
3. **Write the text last, as a sharpener.** Compress the verbal
   line. Don't repeat it.
4. **Pressure-test alignment.** If a viewer watches muted, do they
   get the hook? If they look away, does the voice still pull them
   back? If they're glancing while scrolling, does the text alone
   make them pause?

A misaligned three-layer hook reads as confused. An aligned one
reads as inevitable. The difference is almost never the cleverness
of the line. It's whether the layers agree.

See `assets/three-layer-worksheet.md` for a side-by-side sheet to
fill in before shooting.

Carousel outline template

For static, swipeable formats (Instagram, LinkedIn). The job of every slide is to
earn the swipe to the next. One idea per slide, big readable text, generous
margins inside the safe zone.

```
TOPIC:
AUDIENCE:
GOAL:              (saves / shares / follows)
SLIDE COUNT:       (5-10)

SLIDE 1: HOOK
  • One bold idea or promise, large type. No logo, no intro.
  • This is a hook (see references/hooks.md), not a title page.

SLIDE 2: THE STAKES / WHY CARE
  • Why this matters now, or the cost of getting it wrong.

SLIDES 3..n-2: ONE POINT PER SLIDE
  • Slide 3: strongest practical point (front-loaded to survive early drop).
  • Slide 4: …
  • Slide 5: …
  • Keep each to a single idea + one supporting line.

SLIDE n-1: SUMMARY / RECAP
  • The whole thing distilled to a saveable list. This is the "save" slide.

SLIDE n: CTA
  • One ask: save, follow for more, or comment a keyword.
```

Notes:
- Caption (post text): repeat the hook in the first line. It shows in the feed
  before the image fully registers.
- If a slide has two ideas, split it. If a slide has none, cut it.

Hook checklist

Run any candidate hook through this. A strong hook clears most of these; if it
fails the first three, rewrite it before going further.

- [ ] **Lands in ~2 seconds** when said out loud. No setup, no "hey guys."
- [ ] **Leads with payoff or stake**, not context or brand.
- [ ] **Concrete**: has a specific noun, number, or named stake.
- [ ] **Opens a loop or states a consequence** the viewer needs resolved.
- [ ] **Reads as a hook on mute** (works as on-screen text alone).
- [ ] **Promise is one the video can actually pay off** (no orphan clickbait).
- [ ] **Targeted enough** that the right viewer feels "this is for me."
- [ ] **Distinct archetype** from the other options offered (diversity, not
      variations).

Fast upgrades when a hook is weak:
- Add a number or a dollar/time figure.
- Name the exact viewer ("if you [situation]…").
- Cut everything before the first interesting word.
- Swap a vague benefit for a concrete result.
- Turn a statement into a withheld reveal ("I won't say the brand, but…").

Demo
- **For:** showing a product/result in action.
- **Hook:** the result or the problem, shown immediately (in media res).
- **Structure:** problem/result tease → product in action → transformation → CTA.
  Show, don't narrate. The visual carries it.
- **Length:** 10–30s.
- **Failure mode:** explaining before showing; slow setup.

Before / after
- **For:** transformations of any kind.
- **Hook:** flash the "after" first, then rewind to "before" (in media res).
- **Structure:** after tease → before → process (fast) → after (full) → CTA.
- **Length:** 10–25s.
- **Failure mode:** weak/unclear contrast; process too long.

Archetypes

1. **Curiosity gap.** Name the existence of an answer without giving it.
   *"Nobody tells you the one thing that actually decides whether this works."*
   Use when the payoff is genuinely non-obvious. Don't fake the gap.

2. **Withhold / product-tease.** Show the result or the effect, hold back the
   product or method. *"I'm not going to say the brand, but my [result] is
   unreal."* This is the dominant save-driving mechanic: viewers stay to find out
   what it is, and the comments fill with "what is it?" Use when the reveal is the
   value. (Don't withhold so long it feels like bait.)

3. **Stakes / consequence.** Frame a cost of not watching. *"Stop doing [common
   thing] if you actually want [outcome]."* Use for advice or education.

4. **Bold or contrarian claim.** Stake a position against the consensus.
   *"Morning routines are why you're tired. Here's the fix."* Must be defensible
   in the payoff, or trust dies.

5. **Direct call-out.** Name the exact viewer. *"If you have [specific
   situation], this is for you."* Narrows reach but spikes relevance and saves.

6. **Mistake / cost confession.** *"I wasted $2,000 and 6 months so you don't
   have to."* Specificity (the number) does the work.

7. **Number / listicle.** *"3 things I wish I knew before [thing]."* Sets a clear
   container, and pairs well with fast pacing and on-screen counters.

8. **In media res.** Start mid-action or mid-result, explain after. Good for
   demos and before/afters where the visual *is* the hook.

9. **Question / POV.** *"Why does no one talk about [surprising thing]?"* Use
   sparingly. It's weaker than a claim unless the question is genuinely sharp.

10. **Social proof / result-first.** *"Everyone keeps asking how I did this."*
    Borrows momentum from implied demand.

Pairing hooks to payoff

Every hook makes a promise. Before finalizing, check the script actually delivers
on it within the first few seconds of the body, and fully by the payoff. If it
can't, change the hook, not the truth.

How the algorithm tests you (mental model)

Most platforms show a new post to a small group first, then expand only if the
early signals are strong. So the first cohort's behavior, whether they finish,
loop, save, and share, decides whether anything else happens. This is why the
hook and the first loop matter more than everything after them combined. Optimize
for *passing the test*, not for the dream of the final view count.

How distribution gets decided (community-observed heuristics)

These are patterns creators report, **not published platform rules**. They shift
often and some are folklore. Treat them as directional, optimize for the
underlying signal, and defer to your own analytics over any number here.

- **Completion is the master signal.** On YouTube Shorts it surfaces as
  *Viewed-vs-Swiped-Away* (VVSA), the share who watch rather than swipe; higher
  scales further. Average View Duration (AVD) matters too. Don't chase a specific
  percentage; chase "no reason to swipe."
- **Length follows retention, not a target.** Longer Shorts (up to ~50–60s) can
  earn more total watch time *only if* retention holds across the extra seconds. A
  long video that sags loses to a tight short one, so never pad to hit a length.
- **TikTok tests with a seed group first.** A new post is shown to a small cohort;
  strong completion and repeat-loops trigger wider pushes. The first seconds and
  the loop decide almost everything.
- **Instagram Reels rewards shares and saves.** They trigger reach to
  *non-followers*. Build in a reason to send it to a friend or save it for later.
- **YouTube Shorts is also a search engine.** Shorts surface in search for months,
  so titles, descriptions, and keywords keep earning views long after posting.

What this skill does

1. Picks up the brand and product from the user's Advibly account
2. Generates a realistic AI creator reference image with `advibly_generate_image` (gpt-image-2)
3. Writes a 5-shot direct response script with dialogue for each scene
4. Builds a storyboard: one start frame per shot (gpt-image-2, creator + product as references), shown to the user for approval before any video renders
5. Animates each approved frame with `advibly_generate_video` (Gemini Omni Flash image-to-video, 9:16, native audio: the creator speaks the dialogue)
6. Assembles the clips into one finished vertical ad with one `advibly_render_composition` call

Every generation spends the account's Advibly credits. Renders are the expensive part; script edits are free. Get the dialogue right before generating video.

Step 1 - Intake

Collect, in order of priority:

1. **Brand** - `advibly_list_brands`. One brand: use it. Several: ask which. None: send the user to advibly.com/onboarding.
2. **Brand context** - `advibly_get_brand` for identity, tone, and the research brief. Use it to sharpen dialogue voice and audience targeting. Call `advibly_get_brand_dossier` only if you need objections, competitor claims, or voice-of-customer quotes for the script.
3. **Product** - the physical thing the creator holds on camera.
   - Store brands (`brand_type: "ecom_store"`): `advibly_get_products`, pick the product with the user, and note its image URL. Do NOT pass `product_id` to the video tool later; this skill needs the photo as a reference image, not a start frame (see Step 4).
   - Other brand types: check `advibly_get_assets` for a usable product photo, or ask the user to provide one (`advibly_upload_asset`). If there is no physical product (SaaS, apps), the ad becomes a to-camera testimonial without product-in-hand shots; screenshots from the asset library can appear as phone-in-hand content instead.
4. **Ad angle** - pick one or ask:
   - `testimonial` - creator speaks to camera about results (default)
   - `car/on-the-go` - creator in car or commuting, convenience angle
   - `unboxing` - creator reveals and reacts to product
   - `lifestyle-demo` - creator using product in natural environment
   - `problem-solution` - before state, product intro, after state
5. **Creator description** - brief description (age, gender, vibe). If not provided, match an archetype from `references/characters.md` to the product category. Default: "27-year-old woman, relatable fitness-oriented, not model-perfect."

Once the brand is resolved, create the run's project with `advibly_create_project` (`brand_id` plus a deliverable-shaped name like "Acme UGC testimonial ad") and pass the returned `project_id` on every generate call in this workflow (creator image, storyboard frames, clips, the final composition) so the whole run shows as one tile in the user's library. If the user is continuing an earlier run, find its project with `advibly_list_projects` instead of creating a duplicate.

Do not ask for everything at once. Brand plus angle is enough to start; fill the rest from the brand data and sensible defaults.

Step 3 - Write the 5-shot direct response script

For the chosen angle, write the complete shot list (per-angle breakdowns in `references/angles.md`). Each shot gets:

```
Shot N/5 - [Shot name]
Environment: [where the creator is, specific room/setting/context]
Action: [exactly what is happening, one action only per shot]
Creator on camera: [yes / no (B-roll)]
Product in frame: [yes/no, and if yes, how]
Dialogue: [what the creator says, ~3 words per second, UGC voice; B-roll dialogue plays as voice-over]
```

Most shots feature the creator on camera. A shot can be B-roll instead (hands-only close-up, product on a counter, environment detail) when showing the creator adds nothing: common for problem-agitation and transformation beats. Mark it in the shot list; B-roll changes how its storyboard frame is generated in Step 4.

**Direct response structure (default, testimonial angle):**

| Shot | Job | Environment | Product |
|------|-----|-------------|---------|
| 1 - Hook | Stop the scroll with a single claim | Kitchen / bathroom / neutral | Yes, held toward camera |
| 2 - Problem | Make the viewer feel the pain | Bedroom / desk / car | No |
| 3 - Discovery | Introduce the product naturally | Kitchen / bathroom | Yes, opening/interacting |
| 4 - Transformation | Show the result. Specific, not vague | Gym / outdoors / work | No |
| 5 - CTA | One action, remove friction | Back to Shot 1 environment | Yes, held toward camera |

**Dialogue rules:**
- UGC voice: "Okay I need to talk about this," not "Introducing our new product"
- ~3 words per second of screen time. An 8-second shot = ~24 words max
- First line is the hook and must work without sound (captions carry it on autoplay)
- Product name appears in Shot 3 or later, never Shot 1
- CTA is punchy: "link is below" / "you literally have nothing to lose," never "shop now" or "buy today"
- Mirror the brand's tone of voice from `advibly_get_brand`, but keep it person-casual, not brand-polished

Show the user the shot list with the dialogue before generating the storyboard. Dialogue changes are free; renders cost credits. Then proceed.

Step 5 - Animate the five clips

For each approved frame, call `advibly_generate_video` with Gemini Omni Flash in image-to-video mode. The model generates native audio, so the creator speaks the dialogue in the clip itself.

```
advibly_generate_video
  prompt: <shot prompt, see below>
  brand_id: <brand id>
  project_id: <project id>
  model: "gemini-omni-flash"
  aspect_ratio: "9:16"
  duration: 8
  start_image_url: <the shot's approved storyboard frame URL>
```

Rules:
- `start_image_url` is the approved frame. Do NOT also pass `reference_image_urls`: that switches the pipeline to reference-to-video and the frame stops being the opening frame. The frame already carries the creator and product likeness.
- Never pass `product_id` to this tool: it would replace your storyboard frame with the raw product photo as the opening frame.
- The prompt now describes motion and speech, not composition (the frame owns composition): what the creator does from this frozen moment, and the dialogue.

**Shot prompt structure:**

```
The scene comes to life from this frame. [Action, one action only, continuing naturally from the pose]. Speaking directly to lens: "[dialogue]." [For B-roll: no one on camera, voice-over says: "[dialogue]."] Handheld feel, slight camera shake, candid, natural skin texture, imperfect framing. The person, outfit, product, and environment stay exactly as in the first frame.
```

Full modifier tables, lighting options, and hallucination workarounds are in `references/prompting.md`. The non-negotiable modifiers on every shot: `handheld feel, slight camera shake`, `candid`, `natural skin texture`, `imperfect framing`. Without them Omni Flash defaults to polished commercial output, which is the opposite of what converts.

Execution notes:
- Fire the five calls in parallel if the client supports it; video renders take a few minutes each.
- Each call waits ~40s and usually returns `status: pending` with a `generation_id`. Collect finished URLs with `advibly_get_generation` (`wait: true`), one per generation.
- `content_rejected` means the content policy blocked the prompt: rework the wording, do not retry verbatim.
- `insufficient_credits`: call `advibly_buy_credits` and share the checkout link; credits apply automatically after payment.
- If one shot comes back wrong (garbled label, weird hands, off dialogue), regenerate only that shot.

Step 7 - Optional: publish

If the user wants to post the ad, `advibly_social_list_accounts` shows the brand's connected platforms and `advibly_social_create_post` publishes or schedules it (attach via `generation_ids` for single clips, or `media_urls` for a stitched file uploaded with `advibly_upload_asset`). Only offer this after the user has seen the final ad.

Ad Angles Reference

Shot-by-shot breakdowns for all five preset angles. Each includes visual direction, dialogue patterns, product reference notes, and which shots are creator-only vs product-forward. Shots run 8 seconds each on Gemini Omni Flash (10 if the dialogue needs the room).

Any shot can be reframed as B-roll (hands-only close-up, product on a surface, environment detail) when the creator's face adds nothing; problem-agitation and transformation beats are the usual candidates. B-roll dialogue plays as voice-over, and the shot's storyboard frame is generated without the creator reference.

Angle 1 - Testimonial (Default)

Best for: supplements, skincare, any product with a specific result claim.
Structure: 5 shots, 8 seconds each, ~40 seconds total.

**Shot 1 - Hook**
Environment: Kitchen, bathroom, or any clean neutral interior
Action: Creator holds product toward camera
Product: Yes, held with both hands, label visible
Dialogue pattern: Single result claim. "I've been [doing X] for [timeframe] and [specific result]."
Lighting: Soft window light
Notes: This is your scroll-stopper. One claim. No setup. Product visible immediately.

**Shot 2 - Problem agitation**
Environment: Bedroom (morning), desk (work), or any relatable "before" context
Action: Creator without product; tired, overwhelmed, or frustrated expression
Product: No
Dialogue pattern: Describe the before state specifically. "I used to [specific pain]. Before [time/action], I was already [negative state]."
Lighting: Slightly dimmer; morning light through curtains, overhead only
Notes: Make the pain specific. "Tired all the time" is weak. "Hitting a wall at 2pm every single day" is strong.

**Shot 3 - Discovery**
Environment: Kitchen, bathroom, or where they would realistically find the product
Action: Creator opens, picks up, or interacts with product
Product: Yes, opening/rotating/examining
Dialogue pattern: Natural, slightly skeptical intro to product. "A friend told me about [product/category] and I figured [low-stakes reason to try it]."
Lighting: Warm, natural
Notes: Product name appears here for the first time. Don't pitch, introduce naturally.

**Shot 4 - Transformation**
Environment: Gym, outdoors, work, anywhere active
Action: Creator in motion or looking/feeling visibly different
Product: No
Dialogue pattern: Specific result at a specific time. "By [timeframe] I noticed [specific change]. [Timeframe 2]: [bigger specific change]."
Lighting: Natural, active environment appropriate
Notes: "I feel better" is weak. "Waking up before my alarm" is strong. Specificity = believability.

**Shot 5 - CTA**
Environment: Back to Shot 1 environment; consistency signals confidence
Action: Creator holds product toward camera, slight smile
Product: Yes, held toward camera, label visible
Dialogue pattern: One action, remove friction. "If you're [brief pain restate], [try it for timeframe]. [Link/access note]. [Risk removal: money back / nothing to lose]."
Lighting: Match Shot 1
Notes: Never "shop now." "Link is below" or "I'll link it" reads as UGC. "Shop now" reads as ad.

---

Angle 2 - Car / On-the-Go

Best for: supplements, snacks, energy products, convenience-angle products, anything portable.
Structure: 4 shots, 8 seconds each, ~30 seconds total.
Key environment: Car interior throughout; consistency is the visual hook.

**Shot 1 - Hook in car**
Environment: Driver's seat, residential area visible through window
Action: Creator holds product toward camera
Product: Yes, product visible, appropriate for the category
Dialogue pattern: Convenience setup. "Okay, I used to [messy/complicated old routine] in my car."
Lighting: Soft overcast daylight through windshield / warm afternoon side light

**Shot 2 - Problem demo**
Environment: Same car, passenger seat or bag visible
Action: Creator mimes the old routine: mixing, measuring, spilling, etc.
Product: No (or old product if applicable)
Dialogue pattern: Describe the chaos specifically. "[Action] rolling everywhere, [mess] going everywhere."
Lighting: Match Shot 1

**Shot 3 - Product demo**
Environment: Same car
Action: Creator opens product or holds it up (hold-and-show, no consumption on camera)
Product: Yes, interaction with product
Dialogue pattern: Simple, punchy contrast. "Now I just [simple action]. No [pain 1], no [pain 2], no [pain 3]."
Lighting: Match Shot 1

**Shot 4 - Social proof / volume**
Environment: Same car, bag or purse visible on passenger seat
Action: Creator pulls multiple units out of bag, holds them toward camera
Product: Yes, multiple units
Dialogue pattern: "I have [number] of these in my bag at all times. [Simple why]."
Lighting: Match Shot 1
Notes: The "I stock up" shot is a strong conversion signal. It implies the creator bought multiple, not gifted one.

---

Angle 4 - Lifestyle Demo

Best for: apparel, home goods, drinkware, anything that fits into a daily routine.
Structure: 5 shots, 8 seconds each, ~40 seconds total.

**Shot 1 - Environment establish**
Environment: The lifestyle context: kitchen, gym, home office, outdoor space
Action: Creator in scene, product incidentally visible but not featured
Product: In background or held casually
Dialogue pattern: Context setup. "My morning routine has completely changed since I started using [product category]."
Notes: This shot establishes "this is a real life" before the product reveal.

**Shot 2 - Product intro**
Environment: Same or adjacent space
Action: Creator picks up, holds, or shows product
Product: Yes, product forward
Dialogue pattern: Natural intro. "This is the [product name]. I've been using it for [timeframe]."

**Shot 3 - Use case A**
Environment: In context: at desk, in kitchen, at gym, etc.
Action: Creator using product in the relevant context
Product: In use
Dialogue pattern: First benefit. "[Use case] is so much [better/easier/different] now."

**Shot 4 - Use case B**
Environment: Different context or same with different application
Action: Different use of same product
Product: In use
Dialogue pattern: Second benefit. "And then [second use case], which I wasn't even expecting."

**Shot 5 - Wrap / CTA**
Environment: Back to Shot 1 environment
Action: Creator holds product, direct to camera
Product: Yes, held toward camera
Dialogue pattern: "Honestly one of the best purchases I've made this year. Link is below."

---

Angle 5 - Problem-Solution

Best for: any product that solves a specific, nameable problem. Especially effective for functional products: organizers, tools, ergonomic accessories, cleaning products.
Structure: 4 shots, 8 seconds each, ~30 seconds total.

**Shot 1 - Problem state**
Environment: Where the problem occurs: cluttered desk, messy drawer, uncomfortable workspace
Action: Creator in the problem situation, frustrated or resigned
Product: Not visible yet
Dialogue pattern: Name the problem with specificity. "I have been dealing with [specific problem] for [timeframe] and I genuinely thought it was just [resigned acceptance]."
Notes: The more specific the problem, the more qualified the audience. "Messy desk" is weak. "My charging cables were taking up an entire drawer" is strong.

**Shot 2 - Product reveal**
Environment: Same space but before the solution is installed/used
Action: Creator holds product toward camera, first reveal
Product: Yes, clear reveal, packaging or product itself
Dialogue pattern: Introduce without overselling. "A friend sent me [product name]. I was like, okay, this is a stretch."

**Shot 3 - Demo**
Environment: Same space, product in use
Action: Creator demonstrates the solution in action
Product: In use, solving the problem
Dialogue pattern: Walk through what it does. "You [action with product], and then [result]. That's it. That's the whole thing."
Notes: Keep the demo to one action. Two actions in one shot gets confusing. Show the single clearest benefit.

**Shot 4 - After state / CTA**
Environment: Same space, now with the problem solved
Action: Creator shows the improved state, holds product toward camera
Product: Yes, held or visible in the improved environment
Dialogue pattern: Result + CTA. "[Specific result], [timeframe] later. I'll link this below. You need it."

Required Style Modifiers (Every Shot)

Add all of these to every prompt:

| Modifier | What it does |
|----------|-------------|
| `handheld feel, slight camera shake` | Removes the locked-off tripod look |
| `candid` | One of the strongest realism signals; tells the model this is not a set piece |
| `natural skin texture` | Prevents the "plastic skin" AI tell |
| `imperfect framing` | The model centers everything without this; real UGC is never perfectly composed |
| `[environment-specific lighting]` | Replaces the default studio light inference |

**Lighting options by environment:**
- Kitchen: `soft morning window light` / `warm overhead kitchen light`
- Car: `soft overcast daylight through windshield` / `warm afternoon side light`
- Bathroom: `natural vanity light` / `warm bathroom overhead`
- Gym: `overhead fluorescent, slightly harsh` / `natural light from window`
- Outdoors: `overcast natural light` / `direct afternoon sun, slight squint`
- Bedroom: `soft morning light through curtains` / `bedside lamp, warm`

Grounded Inputs

Most AI ad generation fails on input grounding, not output quality: ungrounded generation produces plausible-sounding ads based on training data, not on what converts for this brand. For scaled production (Mode 3), maintain a durable inputs corpus:

```
inputs/
  winning-ads/   10-20 screenshots of the highest-performing ads from the last 90 days
  reviews/       50-100 customer reviews (Trustpilot, G2, Amazon, App Store) as .md/.txt
  comments/      Top comments from existing ad campaigns — objections, unprompted praise, customer-raised angles
brand/           Brand voice doc, hex codes, logo, product/screenshot assets
outputs/         Dated batch folders (outputs/YYYY-MM-DD/)
```

**Why each input matters:**
- **Winning ads** carry the hooks, structures, and angles already proven for this brand
- **Reviews** carry the exact language buyers use for pain, transformation, and unexpected benefits — pull copy from them verbatim rather than paraphrasing
- **Ad comments** are the most-skipped and highest-value input: objections ("but does it work for X?") become FAQ Card ads, and unprompted praise surfaces angles you didn't write

**Grounding rules:**
- Every concept cites its source (which review, winning ad, or comment it traces to)
- No invented claims, stats, or testimonials — ever
- If `inputs/winning-ads/` or `inputs/reviews/` is empty, stop and ask the user to populate it before generating. Do not generate ungrounded concepts as a fallback.
- Inputs decay: refresh `inputs/winning-ads/` as new ads scale; refresh `inputs/reviews/` and `inputs/comments/` monthly

Common Mistakes

- **Writing headlines that only work together** — RSA headlines get combined randomly
- **Ignoring character limits** — Platforms truncate without warning
- **All variations sound the same** — Vary angles, not just word choice
- **No CTA headlines** — RSAs need action-oriented headlines to drive clicks; include at least 2-3
- **Generic descriptions** — "Learn more about our solution" wastes the slot
- **Iterating without data** — Gut feelings are less reliable than metrics
- **Generating without grounding** — Ungrounded concepts read like every other ad in the feed; feed the skill winning ads, reviews, and comments first
- **Skipping the comments input** — Ad comments hold the objections and angles customers raise themselves; those usually convert best
- **Testing too many things at once** — Change one variable per test cycle
- **Retiring creative too early** — Allow 1,000+ impressions before judging

Occam's Razor
The simplest explanation is usually correct. Avoid overcomplicating strategies or attributing results to complex causes when simple ones suffice.

**Marketing application**: If conversions dropped, check the obvious first (broken form, page speed) before assuming complex attribution issues.

Local vs. Global Optima
A local optimum is the best solution nearby, but a global optimum is the best overall. Don't get stuck optimizing the wrong thing.

**Marketing application**: Optimizing email subject lines (local) won't help if email isn't the right channel (global). Zoom out before zooming in.

Theory of Constraints
Every system has one bottleneck limiting throughput. Find and fix that constraint before optimizing elsewhere.

**Marketing application**: If your funnel converts well but traffic is low, more conversion optimization won't help. Fix the traffic bottleneck first.

Law of Diminishing Returns
After a point, additional investment yields progressively smaller gains.

**Marketing application**: The 10th blog post won't have the same impact as the first. Know when to diversify rather than double down.

Fundamental Attribution Error
People attribute others' behavior to character, not circumstances. "They didn't buy because they're not serious" vs. "The checkout was confusing."

**Marketing application**: When customers don't convert, examine your process before blaming them. The problem is usually situational, not personal.

Mere Exposure Effect
People prefer things they've seen before. Familiarity breeds liking.

**Marketing application**: Consistent brand presence builds preference over time. Repetition across channels creates comfort and trust.

Reciprocity Principle
People feel obligated to return favors. Give first, and people want to give back.

**Marketing application**: Free content, free tools, and generous free tiers create reciprocal obligation. Give value before asking for anything.

Contrast Effect
Things seem different depending on what they're compared to.

**Marketing application**: Show the "before" state clearly. The contrast with your "after" makes improvements vivid.

---

AIDA Funnel
Attention → Interest → Desire → Action. The classic customer journey model.

**Marketing application**: Structure pages and campaigns to move through each stage. Capture attention before building desire.

Rule of 7
Prospects need roughly 7 touchpoints before converting. One ad rarely converts; sustained presence does.

**Marketing application**: Build multi-touch campaigns across channels. Retargeting, email sequences, and consistent presence compound.

Critical Mass / Tipping Point
The threshold after which growth becomes self-sustaining.

**Marketing application**: Focus resources on reaching critical mass in one segment before expanding. Depth before breadth.

Common Mistakes

1. **Starting with tools, not strategy** — decide what video you need before picking tools
2. **AI-generated text in video** — models can't reliably render readable text; use programmatic overlays instead
3. **Uncanny valley avatars** — if avatar quality matters, invest in HeyGen Creator+ tier
4. **No captions** — 85% of social video is watched without sound
5. **Wrong aspect ratio** — 9:16 for social, 16:9 for YouTube/website, 1:1 for feeds
6. **Over-producing** — authentic often outperforms polished, especially on TikTok

When to produce one

- **Presenting a batch for approval** — after Mode 1 or Mode 3 generation, package the top concepts into a review page instead of (or alongside) `INDEX.md`. Picking 5 of 50 is a *visual* decision; a client shouldn't have to read markdown to make it.
- **Pitching a whitelist / co-branded partnership** — the format the source pattern was built for: show the partner exactly what the ad looks like under each handle, with the rollout mechanics spelled out.
- **A monthly slate review** (Mode 4) — render the slate's concepts so the account-state call and the pick happen off one link.

Don't produce one for a single headline tweak or a quick internal gut-check — the markdown output is faster. Reach for the review page when a human who isn't you needs to choose.

The frame storyboard = a carousel narrative arc

A concept's `frames` are its storyboard. Label each frame by the *job it does*, not its content — `Hook`, `The problem`, `The results`, `The ask`. This is the same narrative-arc thinking as the carousel frameworks: a proof-led concept is literally Hook → Problem → Mechanism → Results → Context → Ask. For the five reusable carousel arcs (Value-Stack, Problem-Proof, Hack List, Rant Callout, Demo Walkthrough), see `carousel-frameworks.md` in the **social** skill and pick the arc that fits the angle before writing frames.

Images vs. placeholders

Every frame renders one of two ways:
- **`image` provided** — the real creative (from the Mode 3 `images/` folder, a hosted URL, or a data URI) fills the frame.
- **`image` omitted** — a styled placeholder shows the frame `label` + `prompt`. This is the intended state for concepts that are copy + image-prompt but not yet rendered to image — the review page is useful *before* images exist, and stays useful as they get filled in.

Ship review pages with placeholders freely; they communicate the concept. Swap in images as they're generated.

Common mistakes

- **Too many concepts** — 2–4 tabs is a decision; 10 is a menu nobody finishes. Curate before you present.
- **Unlabeled or content-labeled frames** — label by narrative job (`The proof`), not by what's pictured (`Table screenshot`).
- **Missing or dishonest grounding** — every concept discloses what's real; illustrative proof is labeled illustrative.
- **Editing the render code** — everything is data-driven; if something won't show, it's a `DATA` field, not the JS.
- **Absolute image paths** — keep image paths relative so the output folder can be zipped, moved, or hosted intact.

Step 2: Turn Signals into Evidence-Ranked Concepts

A **concept** is one testable creative hypothesis: *segment × motivation × angle × format*, with its evidence attached. "UGC for moms" is not a concept; "new-parent insomniacs (per 40+ reviews mentioning 3am feeds) × 'quiet enough to not wake the baby' × before/after demo × POV night-shot video" is.

Rank every concept by the strongest evidence supporting it:

| Tier | Evidence | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Your own account: a converting ad with the same angle/segment | Strongest — iterate and extend |
| 2 | Your customers verbatim: recurring review/call language | Strong — build new creative on it |
| 3 | Competitor creative running 60+ days (presumed working) | Good — adapt the angle, never the ad |
| 4 | Organic engagement in the niche (unpaid views/saves on the theme) | Moderate — validate cheaply first |
| 5 | Cross-niche pattern (worked in an adjacent category) | Weak — icebox until corroborated |
| 6 | Team hunch, no external signal | Weakest — low-fi test or drop |

Higher evidence earns roadmap *priority* — an earlier slot in the slate. Production tier is a separate call, set by validation strength, existing assets, capacity, and risk: even a tier-2 customer-language concept starts low-fidelity until it shows a funnel signal. Hunches aren't banned — they're just cheap and last.

Step 3: Branch on Account State

The right creative mix depends on which of two states the account is in. Diagnose before roadmapping — a plan built for the wrong state wastes the month.

**Exploration state** — nothing (or nothing new) is working:
- Go **wide, not deep**: mostly net-new concepts across different segments and angles; keep iterations to a small minority — iterating on losers multiplies losers
- **Redefine "win" per-metric**: with no full-funnel winners, a single-metric improvement (a hold-rate lift, a CPC drop, a CVR bump) on any test is a hit worth pulling on — see the diagnostic funnel
- Iterate **only on hits**; everything else stays exploratory
- Common root causes to check while testing: the creative is boring (safe, seen-before), the message is overcomplicated, the offer/UVP is unclear, or CPMs are punishing a too-narrow audience

**Scaling state** — one or more concepts are converting profitably:
- Go **deep on the winner** while it's open: a winner-led slate of visually-distinct variations of the winning concept (same message, new execution — near-duplicates mostly cannibalize the original's reach and teach you nothing new, so variations must look meaningfully different), plus a remix lane (tonal/emotional re-executions of it) and sub-angle probes drilling *into* the winning segment; tune the split to budget, fatigue speed, and production velocity
- Keep a small exploration allocation alive even mid-scale — winners fatigue, and the next winner is rarely an iteration of the current one
- Speed matters more in this state: a scaling window is finite

Retro rules:

- **Judge concepts, not ads.** Three executions of one concept failing says the concept is wrong; one failing says the execution was.
- **Read the funnel, not the ROAS column.** The diagnostic funnel says *what* to fix; ROAS alone says only *that* something is broken.
- **Enough data before verdicts** — respect the impression/spend thresholds in Common Mistakes and the **ads** skill's decision systems; a two-day read is a coin flip.
- **Every learning lands somewhere**: icebox update, evidence re-rank, or kill. A retro that changes nothing in the roadmap was a meeting, not a retro.

To run this loop on a schedule (retro on the 1st, weekly refresh Mondays, daily batches via Mode 3), see the creative loops in **marketing-loops**.

Failure Modes

- **Roadmapping without a diagnosis** — a slate built before reading the three signals is a wish list; testing without a diagnosis isn't strategy
- **Iteration-heavy slates in exploration state** — polishing losers while the real problem (angle, offer, audience) goes untested
- **Ignoring capacity** — the plan the team can't produce at quality is a plan to produce slop
- **Evidence-free concepts jumping the queue** — the loudest stakeholder's hunch ships as a T3 shoot while tier-2 customer language sits in the icebox
- **Retro as theater** — winners celebrated, nothing re-ranked, icebox untouched
- **Scaling-state complacency** — 100% of the slate on winner variations; when the winner fatigues, the pipeline is empty

The Generation Pipeline

Work top-down; hooks written without the upstream steps read like everyone else's ads.

```
Segment → Motivation → Format → Hook (three components)
```

1. **Segment** — which specific buyer this hook addresses. Not the whole ICP: a slice with a shared situation (from the Grounded Inputs corpus: reviews, comments, sales-call language). The narrower the segment, the sharper the hook.
2. **Motivation** — the single pain, desire, or objection that moves this segment, in *their* words. Pull verbatim phrases from reviews and comments; the corpus language always outperforms marketing paraphrase.
3. **Format** — the delivery vehicle: street interview, POV selfie, screen recording, unboxing, side-by-side demo, text-on-screen static, founder-to-camera, reaction stitch. Pick the format *before* writing the line — the same motivation reads completely differently as a street-interview answer vs. a confession-to-camera.
4. **Hook** — now write the three components for this segment × motivation × format cell.

**Output as a hook matrix** so coverage is visible:

```
| # | Segment | Motivation (verbatim source) | Format | Visual action | Spoken line | Caption |
```

Generate across the matrix, not down a single column — ten hooks for ten segment×motivation cells beat thirty rewordings of one cell. This is the same angle-diversity principle as the static template library: matrix diversity is audience diversity.

Hook Opening Moves

A menu of proven opening structures. Cycle through them like the static templates — don't cluster on favorites:

| Move | Shape | Watch out |
|---|---|---|
| **Curiosity gap** | Withhold the noun: "Nobody tells you what actually causes this" | Must pay off within the ad or it's clickbait that poisons CVR |
| **Bold claim** | A specific, falsifiable statement: "This replaced my entire morning routine" | Needs substantiation on screen or in the on-ramp |
| **First-person confession** | "I was doing [common thing] completely wrong" | Reads fake without lived-in detail |
| **Contrast / before-after** | Two states shown or named in the first beat | The transformation must be visually honest — see compliance notes in SKILL.md |
| **Relatability / POV** | Mirror a hyper-specific situation: "POV: it's 3pm and you're on your fourth coffee" | Specificity is the entire mechanic; generic POV is invisible |
| **Question** | Ask the exact question the buyer types into search or ChatGPT | Use their phrasing verbatim from the corpus |
| **Countdown / gamified** | A timer or on-screen challenge that promises a payoff at the end | Payoff must exist; hold-rate collapses on cheats |
| **Proof-first** | Lead with the receipt — the result screenshot, the stat, the demo money-shot | Strongest when the proof brags by itself |

The Diagnostic Funnel

Each metric in the delivery funnel isolates a different component. When an ad underperforms, read the funnel to find *which part* to fix instead of scrapping the whole ad:

| Stage | Metric | If it's weak, the problem is | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stop | Thumbstop / 3-sec view rate | **Visual action** (and caption) | New visual opening; same everything else |
| Stay | Hold rate (3s → 15s / 50% view) | **The on-ramp** — what follows the hook | Rework seconds 3–15, not the hook |
| Click | CTR | Desire/offer clarity mid-ad | Sharpen the promise, CTA, or proof |
| Convert | CVR post-click | Congruence — the page doesn't continue the ad | Fix the landing page or the claim, per **cro** |

Two rules this table enforces:

- **A great thumbstop is not a great ad.** A clickbait visual that attracts the wrong viewers shows up as high thumbstop + collapsed hold/CVR. Read the whole funnel before declaring a winning hook.
- **One component per iteration.** Change the visual OR the on-ramp OR the offer framing per test cycle — matching the one-variable rule in Common Mistakes.

Concept Angles

Most iMessage ads fit one of six angles. Pick the angle before writing any copy — the most common failure mode ("script is fine but the ad feels off") is an angle mismatch, not bad lines. The strongest hooks share one of three traits: a specific number, a small act of self-trust, or a physically novel product mechanic.

| Angle | The hook attachment | The reveal |
|---|---|---|
| **Result-as-screenshot** | A number that brags by itself — race time, app summary, dashboard stat | "X minutes a day. that's it." |
| **Setup flex** | A photo of your space — tiny apartment gym, race-kit corner, desk setup | "this is the whole setup" |
| **Cancellation moment** | A confirmation receipt — gym cancellation email, "subscription cancelled" page | "$X/mo → $Y/mo. do the math" |
| **Feature-as-punchline** | A short clip of the product mechanic in motion | The mechanic *is* the brand |
| **Friend-asks-friend (inverse)** | The *peer* opens with the wow — "how are you doing this 😭" | *You* reply with the brand |
| **Receipt-as-hook** | A mundane financial document — statement, App Store receipt | A small act of self-trust |

Anatomy of the Ad

```
0:00  Hook attachment lands (the screenshot the whole chat is about)
      ↓ short reactions, 250–450ms apart ("bro no way" / "wait is that real")
0:06  The question — "what app is that??"
      ↓ typing indicator … then the brand-name reply
0:12  The pitch, in texting voice — one or two bubbles max
0:15  The code — "use FREEPACK, first pack's free" (code renders link-underlined)
0:17  Beat of silence, then the closer — "bet" / "ok downloading"
0:18  300ms crossfade → static brand end card: logo, code, tagline (~3s)
```

**Script rules:**

- **8–14 bubbles total.** Shorter reads thin; longer loses the scroll-past viewer.
- **Write in real texting voice.** Lowercase, fragments, one emoji max per message, no marketing adjectives. Read it aloud as two friends — any bubble that sounds like ad copy gets cut.
- **The brand appears once, late.** The thread is about the *result* until someone asks. Naming the brand in bubble two kills the reveal.
- **Pacing has rhythm, not a metronome.** One-word reactions fire 250–450ms apart; sentence replies get 600–900ms of air after them; leave ~600ms of silence before the final reaction so it lands.
- **Typing indicators go before sentence-length peer replies**, optional before short reactions. The indicator appearing is silent (see SFX rules below).
- **The promo code goes inside a bubble**, styled with iOS's link-detection underline, *and* on the end card. Conversational delivery first, reinforcement second.
